Davy's bat, Pteronotus davyi, exhibits a resting metabolic rate of 15.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 15.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at the thermoneutral body temperature typical of active individuals, 38.8 °C [T = 38.8 °C]. This basal oxygen consumption aligns closely with values predicted for small insectivorous bats weighing in the range of five to ten grams as adults. Newborn pups emerge from the uterus weighing just 2.5 grams [Wwb = 2.5 grams], a remarkably low birth mass that reflects the altricial state of the neonate at parturition. The naked, helpless condition of these newborns imposes a considerable energetic burden on the lactating female, who must shuttle between roost and foraging grounds to sustain milk production. Mortality during the first few days of life is likely high, as the small size of the pup limits its thermal inertia and capacity to maintain homeothermy when the mother is absent from the roost.

Females produce a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], and under the stable thermal conditions of the cave roost at 38.8 °C [T = 38.8 °C], they achieve a maximum annual reproductive rate of approximately one litter per year [F_R_i = approximately one litter per year]. The gestation period extends for approximately 60 days [tg = approximately 60 days] under the same body temperature regime of 38.8 °C [T = 38.8 °C], a duration that appears to be intermediate among molossid bats of comparable body size. Following parturition, the pup nurses for a period of 30.5 days following parturition [tx = 30.5 days following parturition] before achieving the trophic independence that defines weaning at a temperature of 38.8 °C [T = 38.8 °C]. At that developmental milestone, the weanling has reached a wet body mass of 7.4 grams [Wwx = 7.4 grams], representing a near-tripling of its birth weight over the course of the weaning period and reflecting the high milk-transfer efficiency typical of small chiropterans.

Juveniles undergo a prolonged period of somatic growth before attaining sexual maturity. Available data indicate that the time since birth at puberty is approximately 365 days [tp = approximately 365 days], meaning that young females typically do not enter their first oestrus until nearly a full year after their own birth, again measured under the thermoneutral body temperature of 38.8 °C [T = 38.8 °C]. This extended interval to reproductive activation is consistent with the pace of life of a small mammal that must reach a substantial proportion of its asymptotic adult size before initiating the energetically costly processes of gestation and lactation. The ultimate adult wet body weight of Pteronotus davyi has been recorded at up to 10 grams [Wwi = up to 10 grams], with most field-captured individuals falling between 8 and 10 grams, suggesting that somatic growth continues for many months after sexual maturation.

The maximum documented lifespan of Davy's bat in the wild has been estimated at 15 years [am = 15 years], a remarkably long duration for an animal of its body size at a temperature of 38.8 °C [T = 38.8 °C]. This longevity estimate was derived from mark-recapture studies of individuals roosting in stable, humid caves where the ambient microclimate remains near 38.8 °C [T = 38.8 °C] throughout the year, a condition that may reduce the metabolic costs of thermoregulation and thereby delay the accumulation of oxidative damage that drives senescence. Such an extended lifespan places Pteronotus davyi among the more long-lived bat species relative to its mass, a pattern commonly attributed to the combination of low extrinsic mortality in protected roost sites and a slow life-history pace shaped by intense age-specific selection for somatic persistence.

Comparative data from related molossid bats further contextualize the life-history strategy of Pteronotus davyi. The wet weight at birth of 2.5 grams [Wwb = 2.5 grams] is comparable to that reported for the Brazilian free-tailed bat, Tadarida brasiliensis, after scaling for differences in adult body mass. Similarly, the gestation period of 60 days [tg = 60 days] recorded at the species' characteristic body temperature of 38.8 °C [T = 38.8 °C] falls within the range observed for other insectivorous bats of equivalent size, suggesting a conserved developmental schedule within the family. The weaning mass of 7.4 grams [Wwx = 7.4 grams] represents roughly three-quarters of the ultimate adult wet weight of 10 grams [Wwi = 10 grams], indicating that nutritional independence occurs at a stage when the juvenile has already attained most of its skeletal dimensions. This pattern of early developmental investment followed by a protracted sub-adult phase is consistent with a life history that prioritizes high juvenile survival in a competitive roosting environment.
